highlights: On 13 September the Military Governor ordered Korean directors to assume full executive charge of all government departments, reducing American personnel to advisory roles while plans advanced for a Korean legislative assembly.

A general railway strike began on 22 September, halting rail transport across South Korea, disrupting coal movement and mail, stranding repatriates, and driving an urban food crisis with rising black-market rice prices.
Military authorities ordered the arrest of Communist leaders Pak Heun Young, Lee Kang Kook and Lee Chu Ha, and the Military Governor suspended three leftist newspapers for inflammatory articles.
Dr. Syngman Rhee escaped unharmed when assassins fired into his automobile on 12 September on the way to an independence rally in Seoul.
Ordinance No. 112 established Korea's first comprehensive Child Labor Law, prohibiting industrial employment of children under fourteen and regulating maximum working hours.

Government-to-government barter trade with Japan began with 24 million yen of minerals and fish shipped for coal and industrial chemicals; Bank of Chosen notes in circulation exceeded 11.3 billion yen.
Cholera in South Korea reached 14,614 cases and 9,474 deaths by 30 September, prompting emergency air shipments of medical supplies during the transport strike.
A Women's Bureau was created in the Department of Public Health and Welfare, and Seoul National University opened its colleges under unified reorganization despite student protests.

sections.summary: Summer grain collections were delayed by the rail strike; the Korea Land Development Company was dissolved and its assets went to government reclamation. Hwasun mine strikes cut coal output; copper smelting at Changhang led mining.

summary: This September 1946 monthly report documents a pivotal period of administrative transition and escalating civil unrest in the United States Army Military Government in Korea (USAMGIK). Markedly, the Military Governor ordered Korean directors to assume full operational control of government departments, relegating American personnel to advisory roles, while preparations advanced for an interim Korean legislative assembly. However, governance was severely disrupted by the outbreak of the nationwide railroad strike on 22 September, which paralyzed ground transportation, stranded repatriates, hampered coal distribution, and precipitated an acute food crisis with skyrocketing black-market rice prices. Authorities responded with emergency airlifts of medical supplies, arrests of top Communist leaders including Pak Heun Young, and suspensions of leftist newspapers. Other significant developments include the promulgation of the Child Labor Law (Ordinance No. 112), commencement of government-to-government barter trade with Japan, structural reorganization of public education into a 6-6 system, opening of Seoul National University colleges, and ongoing efforts to control a lethal cholera epidemic that claimed over 9,400 lives. For historians, the report provides invaluable quantitative data on labor unrest, industrial stagnation, disease mortality, currency expansion, and the administrative mechanics of early South Korean state formation.
